claim: Ca2+ ions are essential for many cellular signaling mechanisms and enter the cytosol mostly through voltage-gated calcium channels.
source: Calcium ions (Ca2+) are essential for many cellular signaling mechanisms and enter the cytosol mostly through voltage-gated calcium channels.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about calcium signaling.

claim: Activity-dependent intracellular calcium concentration in the axonal initial segment was only partially dependent on voltage-gated calcium channels.
source: using high-speed Ca2+ imaging up to 20 kHz in the rat layer five pyramidal neuron axon we found that activity-dependent intracellular calcium concentration ([Ca2+]i) in the axonal initial segment was only partially dependent on voltage-gated calcium channels.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from high-speed calcium imaging experiments.

claim: [Ca2+]i changes were sensitive to the specific voltage-gated sodium (NaV) channel blocker tetrodotoxin.
source: Instead, [Ca2+]i changes were sensitive to the specific voltage-gated sodium (NaV) channel blocker tetrodotoxin.
evidence: This is based on experimental data showing TTX sensitivity of calcium changes.

claim: The optically resolved ICa in the axon initial segment overlapped with the activation kinetics of NaV channels.
source: Consistent with the conjecture that Ca2+ enters through the NaV channel pore, the optically resolved ICa in the axon initial segment overlapped with the activation kinetics of NaV channels
evidence: This is supported by experimental optical recordings of calcium currents.

claim: Heterologous expression of NaV1.2 in HEK-293 cells revealed a tetrodotoxin-sensitive [Ca2+]i rise.
source: heterologous expression of NaV1.2 in HEK-293 cells revealed a tetrodotoxin-sensitive [Ca2+]i rise.
evidence: This is based on experimental data from HEK-293 cell expression experiments.

claim: Computational simulations predicted that axonal [Ca2+]i transients reflect a 0.4% Ca2+ conductivity of NaV channels.
source: Finally, computational simulations predicted that axonal [Ca2+]i transients reflect a 0.4% Ca2+ conductivity of NaV channels.
evidence: This is based on computational modeling and simulations.

claim: Ca2+ permeation through NaV channels provides a submillisecond rapid entry route in NaV-enriched domains of mammalian axons.
source: The findings indicate that Ca2+ permeation through NaV channels provides a submillisecond rapid entry route in NaV-enriched domains of mammalian axons.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental and computational data presented.

claim: In axons, voltage-gated Ca2+ (CaV) channels at presynaptic terminals open in response to a single action potential, raising intracellular Ca2+ concentrations from ~50 nM up to ~10 µM.
source: In axons, voltage-gated Ca2+ (CaV) channels at presynaptic terminals open in response to a single action potential (AP), raising intracellular Ca2+ concentrations ([Ca2+]i) in nanodomains from ~50 nM up to ~10 µM to increase transmitter vesicle release rates by the power of ~4 (Helmchen et al., 1997; Schneggenburger and Neher, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Large and local [Ca2+]i transients are typically observed in the axon initial segment (AIS) and nodes of Ranvier in response to APs.
source: In response to APs, large and local [Ca2+]i transients are typically also observed in the axon initial segment (AIS) and nodes of Ranvier (Callewaert et al., 1996; Bender and Trussell, 2009; Yu et al., 2010; Gründemann and Clark, 2015; Zhang and David, 2016; Clarkson et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Ca2+ currents at the AIS and nodes of Ranvier have been implicated in AP initiation and propagation by a local depolarizing action of the inward current or by activating BKCa channels.
source: At these sites, Ca2+ currents have been implicated in AP initiation and propagation by a local depolarizing action of the inward current or by activating the large conductance, Ca2+- and voltage-dependent K+ (BKCa) channels modulating burst firing probability and limiting frequency-dependent AP failure rates (Bender and Trussell, 2009; Yu et al., 2010; Hirono et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The CaV channel subtypes identified in axons are both cell type- and species-dependent and include the T-, P/Q- or N-type CaV channels.
source: The CaV channel subtypes identified in axons are both cell type- and species-dependent and include the T-, P/Q- or N-type CaV channels (Callewaert et al., 1996; Bender and Trussell, 2009; Yu et al., 2010; Gründemann and Clark, 2015; Zhang and David, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: At the AIS the T-type Ca2+ channel mediates AP-dependent Ca2+ influx.
source: At the AIS in particular the T-type Ca2+ channel mediates AP-dependent Ca2+ influx (Bender and Trussell, 2009; Martinello et al., 2015; Fukaya et al., 2018; Jin et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: In the prefrontal cortical pyramidal neuron AIS about 70% of the AP-evoked [Ca2+]i remains following pharmacological block of T-type CaV channels.
source: However, in the prefrontal cortical pyramidal neuron AIS about 70% of the AP-evoked [Ca2+]i remains following pharmacological block of T-type CaV channels (Clarkson et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Evidence for a clustering of T-type CaV channels at the AIS is ambiguous and immunofluorescence or immuno-gold labeling studies show a density which is comparable to somatodendritic or spine compartments.
source: Furthermore, evidence for a clustering of T-type CaV channels at the AIS is ambiguous and immunofluorescence or immuno-gold labeling studies show a density which is comparable to somatodendritic or spine compartments (McKay et al., 2006; Martinello et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Most AISs contain ER cisternae organelles consisting of stacks of membranes expressing the store-operated ryanodine receptor (RyR), inositol 1,4,5-triphosphate receptor 1(IP3R1) and sarcoplasmic ER Ca2+ ATPase (SERCA) pumps.
source: Most AISs contain ER cisternae organelles consisting of stacks of membranes expressing the store-operated ryanodine receptor (RyR), inositol 1,4,5-triphosphate receptor 1(IP3R1) and sarcoplasmic ER Ca2+ ATPase (SERCA) pumps (Benedeczky et al., 1994; King et al., 2014; Antón-Fernández et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: A reverse mode of operation of the Na+-Ca2+ exchanger (NCX) has been implicated in pathological [Ca2+]i elevations in axons during hypoxia and injury.
source: A reverse mode of operation has not only been implicated in pathological [Ca2+]i elevations in axons during hypoxia and injury (Stys et al., 1991; Iwata et al., 2004)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Reverse mode of NCX operation occurs during trains of APs in nodes and neighboring internodes.
source: but also occurs during trains of APs in nodes and neighboring internodes (Zhang and David, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Studies in the squid giant axon combining electrophysiological recordings with Ca2+ imaging showed that an early component of depolarization-induced Ca2+ entry is tetrodotoxin (TTX)-sensitive.
source: Studies in the squid giant axon combining electrophysiological recordings with Ca2+ imaging showed that an early component of depolarization-induced Ca2+ entry is tetrodotoxin (TTX)-sensitive (Baker et al., 1971; Meves and Vogel, 1973; Brown et al., 1975).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Voltage-clamp recordings from axons and perfusing distinct ionic solutions provided a quantitative estimate that NaV channels may pass divalent Ca2+ ions with permeability ratios (PCa/PNa) up to 0.10.
source: Voltage-clamp recordings from axons and perfusing distinct ionic solutions provided a quantitative estimate that NaV channels may pass divalent Ca2+ ions with permeability ratios (PCa/PNa) up to 0.10 (Hille, 1972; Meves and Vogel, 1973).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Ca2+ permeability of NaV channels has been shown in cardiac cells and hippocampal neurons.
source: Ca2+ permeability of NaV channels has also been shown in cardiac cells and hippocampal neurons (Akaike and Takahashi, 1992; Aggarwal et al., 1997; Santana et al., 1998)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Thick-tufted L5 pyramidal neurons are the largest pyramidal neurons in the cortex and integrate synaptic inputs from all cortical layers.
source: Thick-tufted L5 pyramidal neurons, also called L5B or pyramidal tract neurons, are the largest pyramidal neurons in the cortex and integrate synaptic inputs from all cortical layers, playing a central role in cognitive tasks including perception (Groh et al., 2010; Ramaswamy and Markram, 2015; Takahashi et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Ca2+ signals were observed in the AIS and hot spots separated with regular distances along the axon in response to subthreshold depolarizations.
source: Examination of the spatial profile revealed that Ca2+ signals were observed in the AIS and hot spots separated with regular distances along the axon (locations 2, 4 and 6; Figure 1a).
evidence: This is based on experimental imaging data shown in Figure 1a.

claim: The [Ca2+]i hot spots corresponded to nodes of Ranvier.
source: In order to examine whether the [Ca2+]i hot spots corresponded to nodes of Ranvier, we post-hoc stained for βIV-spectrin and biocytin, and found indeed overlap between subthreshold [Ca2+]i rise and spectrin-enriched sites (Figure 1b).
evidence: This is based on experimental immunostaining data shown in Figure 1b.

claim: AP-induced [Ca2+]i transients were similar between AIS and nodes.
source: Population analysis showed that AP-induced [Ca2+]i transients were similar between AIS and nodes (one-way ANOVA followed by Tukey's multiple comparison test, p<0.0001, differences between all groups were significant (p<0.05) except between AIS and node (p=0.13) and between internode (IN) and dendrites (p=0.85); Figure 1c,d).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 1c,d.

claim: During a-EPSPs the [Ca2+]i transients in the AIS and the first nodes were highly comparable, while [Ca2+]i signals in the internodal and dendritic domains were an order of magnitude smaller.
source: Interestingly, also during a-EPSPs the [Ca2+]i transients in the AIS and the first nodes were highly comparable, while [Ca2+]i signals in the internodal and dendritic domains were an order of magnitude smaller (one-way ANOVA with Tukey's multiple comparison test, p<0.0001, differences between all groups were significant (p<0.0001), except between AIS and node (p=0.38) and IN and Dend (p=0.97); Figure 1a,d).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 1a,d.

claim: Similar experiments in L5 neocortical pyramidal neurons in slices from human temporal cortex revealed a-EPSP evoked Δ[Ca2+]i in the AIS, but not in the dendrite.
source: Similar experiments in L5 neocortical pyramidal neurons in slices from human temporal cortex also revealed a-EPSP evoked Δ[Ca2+]i in the AIS, but not in the dendrite, suggesting that subthreshold sensitive [Ca2+]i transients are conserved across mammalian species (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on experimental data from human tissue shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The thick-tufted L5 pyramidal neuron AIS contains a unique variant of cisternal organelle characterized by a continuous tubular organization of smooth ER, called the giant saccular organelle.
source: The thick-tufted L5 pyramidal neuron AIS contains a unique variant of cisternal organelle characterized by a continuous tubular organization of smooth ER, called the giant saccular organelle (Antón-Fernández et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The cisternal organelle was present along the entire axis of the AIS and spatially overlapped with the subthreshold-evoked [Ca2+]i transients.
source: Triple immunostaining for synpo, Ankyrin G and biocytin confirmed that the cisternal organelle was present along the entire axis of the AIS and spatially overlapped with the subthreshold-evoked [Ca2+]i transients (n = 19; Figure 2a,b).
evidence: This is based on experimental immunostaining data shown in Figure 2a,b.

claim: Subthreshold depolarization-induced Ca2+ transients were present in the nodes, but synaptopodin expression was not detected.
source: However, while subthreshold depolarization-induced Ca2+ transients were present in the nodes, synaptopodin expression was not detected (n = 10 nodes; Figures 1 and 2a).
evidence: This is based on experimental immunostaining and imaging data shown in Figures 1 and 2a.

claim: Blocking Ca2+ release significantly lowered ΔF/F Ca2+ peak transients in the AIS, both for the subthreshold- and AP-evoked [Ca2+]i changes.
source: Blocking Ca2+ release significantly lowered ΔF/F Ca2+ peak transients in the AIS, both for the subthreshold- and AP-evoked [Ca2+]i changes (a-EPSP, 53.2% reduction, p=0.006; AP, 34.3% reduction, p=0.02, one-tailed ratio paired t-tests, n = 5; Figure 2d).
evidence: This is based on experimental data with pharmacological blockers shown in Figure 2d.

claim: Store blockers had no effect on AP-evoked Δ[Ca2+]i in the basal dendrite.
source: Consistent with the AIS-specific location of the giant saccular organelle, store blockers had no effect on AP-evoked Δ[Ca2+]i in the basal dendrite (p=0.48, n = 3; Figure 2d).
evidence: This is based on experimental data with pharmacological blockers shown in Figure 2d.

claim: Blocking Ca2+-store release did not alter the rise- or decay time kinetics in the AIS.
source: However, blocking Ca2+-store release did not alter the rise- or decay time kinetics in the AIS (τact, p=0.52; τde-act, p=0.18, two-tailed paired t-tests, n = 5; Figure 2e).
evidence: This is based on experimental data with pharmacological blockers shown in Figure 2e.

claim: The giant saccular organelle amplifies activity-dependent [Ca2+]i changes selectively in the AIS.
source: These data suggest that the giant saccular organelle amplifies activity-dependent [Ca2+]i changes selectively in the AIS.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on store blockers.

claim: EGTA almost fully abolished the subthreshold-evoked Δ[Ca2+]i (90.7% reduction).
source: Ca2+ imaging at the AIS (OGB-1, 100 µM) showed that EGTA almost fully abolished the subthreshold-evoked Δ[Ca2+]i (90.7% reduction, one-tailed ratio paired t-test, p=0.0031, n = 4; Figure 3a,b).
evidence: This is based on experimental data with EGTA shown in Figure 3a,b.

claim: The AP-generated Δ[Ca2+]i was almost extinguished after bath application of EGTA (92.8% reduction).
source: Similarly, the AP-generated Δ[Ca2+]i was almost extinguished after bath application of EGTA (92.8% reduction, p=0.0011, n = 4; Figure 3a,b).
evidence: This is based on experimental data with EGTA shown in Figure 3a,b.

claim: Bath application of TTA-P2 did not significantly reduce subthreshold Ca2+ signals.
source: However, bath application of the highly selective T-type (CaV3.1–3) blocker TTA-P2 (1 µM, Choe et al., 2011) or nickel (Ni2+, 100 µM) did not significantly reduce Ca2+ signals (one-tailed ratio paired t-tests; TTA-P2, p=0.17, n = 4; Ni2+, p=0.063, n = 5; Figure 3b,c).
evidence: This is based on experimental data with TTA-P2 shown in Figure 3b,c.

claim: SNX-482 did not lead to a reduction in subthreshold [Ca2+]i rise.
source: We next blocked R-type CaV channels, by puffing SNX-482 (500 nM) locally to the AIS, but this did not lead to a reduction in subthreshold [Ca2+]i rise either (SNX-482, p=0.11, n = 3).
evidence: This is based on experimental data with SNX-482.

claim: L-type channels did not affect subthreshold Δ[Ca2+]i.
source: Furthermore, consistent with their more depolarized voltage range of activation, the L-type channels did not affect subthreshold Δ[Ca2+]i (20 µM isradipine, p=0.14; 10 µM nimodipine, p=0.41, both n = 4; Figure 3b)
evidence: This is based on experimental data with L-type channel blockers shown in Figure 3b.

claim: Block of N-type and P/Q-type channels failed to reduce Ca2+ signals.
source: and the block of N-type and P/Q-type channels, by local application of ω-conotoxin MVIIC (2 µM) to the AIS, also failed to reduce Ca2+ signals (p=0.42, n = 5; Figure 3b).
evidence: This is based on experimental data with ω-conotoxin MVIIC shown in Figure 3b.

claim: A combined block of T- and L-type channels did not affect the peak ΔF/F in the AIS.
source: Furthermore, a combined block of T- and L-type channels did not affect the peak ΔF/F in the AIS (TTA-P2 and isradipine, p=0.12, n = 3; Figure 3b).
evidence: This is based on experimental data with combined blockers shown in Figure 3b.

claim: TTA-P2 reduced the peak ΔF/F evoked by a single AP by almost 20%.
source: Although application of the T-type blockers TTA-P2 and Ni2+ was ineffective to block subthreshold [Ca2+]i rise, in the same neurons it did reduce the peak ΔF/F evoked by a single AP by almost 20% (TTA-P2, 18.7%, p=0.021, n = 4; Ni2+, 19.7% block, p=0.013, n = 5; Figure 3b,c).
evidence: This is based on experimental data with TTA-P2 shown in Figure 3b,c.

claim: Isradipine reduced the AP-evoked Δ[Ca2+]i in the AIS by 14.9%.
source: In addition, isradipine reduced the AP-evoked Δ[Ca2+]i in the AIS by 14.9% (isradipine, p=0.0070, n = 4)
evidence: This is based on experimental data with isradipine.

claim: A combined application of T- and L-type channel blockers caused a 27.2% reduction of peak ΔF/F.
source: A combined application of T- and L-type channel blockers (1 µM TTA-P2 and 20 µM isradipine) caused a 27.2% reduction of peak ΔF/F, showing a sublinear summation of two blocking agents (TTA-P2 and isradipine, p=0.0071, n = 5; Figure 3b).
evidence: This is based on experimental data with combined blockers shown in Figure 3b.

claim: The R-type CaV channel blocker SNX-482 did not reduce the AP-evoked Δ[Ca2+]i.
source: In contrast, the R-type CaV channel blocker SNX-482 (500 nM) did not reduce the AP-evoked Δ[Ca2+]i (SNX-482, p=0.29, n = 3; Figure 3b).
evidence: This is based on experimental data with SNX-482 shown in Figure 3b.

claim: Local application of ω-conotoxin MVIIC almost completely abolished the peak ΔF/F in a collateral bouton by 91.5%.
source: As a positive control experiment, we imaged a collateral bouton of the same neuron and used local application of ω-conotoxin MVIIC which almost completely abolished the peak ΔF/F by 91.5%, consistent with the presence of N- and P/Q-type CaV channel subtypes in presynaptic terminals (p=0.021, n = 3; Figure 3b).
evidence: This is based on experimental data with ω-conotoxin MVIIC shown in Figure 3b.

claim: Combined bath application of KB-R7943 and SN-6 showed no change in the subthreshold nor AP-evoked Δ[Ca2+]i.
source: To examine its contribution, we pharmacologically blocked NCX by combined bath application of KB-R7943 (20 µM) and SN-6 (10 µM). The results showed, however, no change in the subthreshold nor AP-evoked Δ[Ca2+]i (two-tailed ratio paired t-tests, a-EPSP, p=0.16; AP, p=0.13, n = 5, respectively; Figure 3b).
evidence: This is based on experimental data with NCX blockers shown in Figure 3b.

claim: Transmembrane Ca2+ influx from the extracellular space is required for activity-evoked Δ[Ca2+]i.
source: In summary, these data show that while transmembrane Ca2+ influx from the extracellular space is required for activity-evoked Δ[Ca2+]i, none of the CaV channels played a role in the subthreshold depolarization, whereas T- and L-type CaV channels partially contributed to the AP-evoked influx.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data with EGTA and channel blockers.

claim: None of the CaV channels played a role in the subthreshold depolarization.
source: In summary, these data show that while transmembrane Ca2+ influx from the extracellular space is required for activity-evoked Δ[Ca2+]i, none of the CaV channels played a role in the subthreshold depolarization, whereas T- and L-type CaV channels partially contributed to the AP-evoked influx.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data with channel blockers.

claim: T- and L-type CaV channels partially contributed to the AP-evoked influx.
source: In summary, these data show that while transmembrane Ca2+ influx from the extracellular space is required for activity-evoked Δ[Ca2+]i, none of the CaV channels played a role in the subthreshold depolarization, whereas T- and L-type CaV channels partially contributed to the AP-evoked influx.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data with channel blockers.

claim: In hippocampal neurons and heart muscle cells, Ca2+ currents have been described which are not blocked by Ni2+ nor by other known CaV channel antagonists, but instead are sensitive to TTX, called ICa(TTX).
source: What could be the source of the remaining component of Ca2+ influx at the AIS? Both in hippocampal neurons and heart muscle cells, Ca2+ currents have been described which are not blocked by Ni2+ nor by other known CaV channel antagonists, but instead are sensitive to the highly selective NaV channel blocker (TTX), and therefore called ICa(TTX) (Akaike and Takahashi, 1992; Aggarwal et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: In Na+-free extracellular solution ICa(TTX) resembles the Na+ current and activates at potentials as negative as –70 mV while peaking at –30 mV.
source: In Na+-free extracellular solution ICa(TTX) resembles the Na+ current and activates at potentials as negative as –70 mV while peaking at –30 mV (Akaike and Takahashi, 1992).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Bath application of TTX almost completely abolished [Ca2+]i elevations, even at depolarizations above the AP threshold (at –54.5 mV, 92.8% block).
source: The results showed that Ca2+ influx was strongly compartmentalized to the AIS and nodal axolemma (Figure 4a) consistent with the a-EPSP evoked OGB-1 transients (Figure 1). Remarkably, bath application of TTX almost completely abolished [Ca2+]i elevations, even at depolarizations above the AP threshold (at –54.5 mV, 92.8% block, Cohen's d: 1.88, two-way ANOVA, p<0.0001, n = 4; Figure 4b,c).
evidence: This is based on experimental data with TTX shown in Figure 4b,c.

claim: With 6 mM QX-314 added to the pipette solution voltage ramps did not evoke Ca2+ transients (at –54.5 mV, 94.8% block).
source: As an alternative to TTX we used the quaternary amine NaV channel inhibitor QX-314, which plugs the open state of the NaV channel from the internal side. Similar to TTX, with 6 mM QX-314 added to the pipette solution voltage ramps did not evoke Ca2+ transients (at –54.5 mV, 94.8% block, Cohen's d: 1.92, control vs. QX-314, p<0.0001, n = 4, TTX vs. QX-314, p=0.97, n = 4; Figure 4c).
evidence: This is based on experimental data with QX-314 shown in Figure 4c.

claim: The near complete block by two distinct NaV channel blockers indicates an important role of NaV channels in mediating subthreshold axonal Ca2+ influx.
source: The near complete block by two distinct NaV channel blockers therefore indicates an important role of NaV channels in mediating subthreshold axonal Ca2+ influx.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data with TTX and QX-314.

claim: TTX blocked 65.5% of the AP-evoked Δ[Ca2+]i.
source: TTX blocked 65.5% of the AP-evoked Δ[Ca2+]i (peak OGB-5N, Cohen's d: 5.49, VC ×2 vs. CC, p<0.0001, n = 8; Figure 5b).
evidence: This is based on experimental data with TTX shown in Figure 5b.

claim: A large fraction of both subthreshold-depolarization and AP-evoked Ca2+ ions enter the axoplasm through TTX-sensitive channels at the AIS.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that a large fraction of both subthreshold-depolarization and AP-evoked Ca2+ ions enter the axoplasm through TTX-sensitive channels at the AIS.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data with TTX.

claim: Using a Na+-sensitive indicator (SBFI) in combination with OGB-5N showed that the two indicators were indistinguishable in their rising phase during an AP.
source: Using a Na+-sensitive indicator (sodium-binding benzofuran isophthalate, SBFI, 1 mM) in combination with OGB-5N (1 mM) showed that the two indicators were indistinguishable in their rising phase during an AP, suggesting that Ca2+ entry at the AIS may be as rapid as Na+ entry (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Near ~20°C and –40 mV, NaV channels open at least one order of magnitude faster compared to the T-type CaV channels (~200 µs vs. ~5 ms).
source: Near ~20°C and –40 mV, NaV channels open at least one order of magnitude faster compared to the T-type CaV channels (~200 µs [Schmidt-Hieber and Bischofberger, 2010] vs. ~5 ms [Perez-Reyes et al., 1998], respectively)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The activation time constant of the total inward current was identical to INa (τtotal = 438.2 µs vs. τNa = 440.3 µs).
source: The activation time constant of the total inward current was identical to INa (single exponential fit τtotal = 438.2 µs vs. τNa = 440.3 µs, one-way ANOVA with Tukey's multiple comparison test, p>0.999, n = 6)
evidence: This is based on experimental data from voltage-clamp recordings.

claim: The total current was substantially faster in comparison to ICaT (τtotal = 438.2 µs vs. τCaT = 4.8 ms).
source: whereas the total current was substantially faster in comparison to ICaT (τtotal = 438.2 µs vs. τCaT = 4.8 ms, p<0.0001, n = 5; Figure 6a).
evidence: This is based on experimental data from voltage-clamp recordings shown in Figure 6a.

claim: The average slope of ICa_opt was significantly faster compared to the activation of ICaT (~500 µs vs. ~2.5 ms).
source: The average slope of ICa_opt was significantly faster compared to the activation of ICaT (~500 µs vs. ~2.5 ms, respectively, one-way ANOVA with Tukey's multiple comparison test, p<0.0001)
evidence: This is based on experimental data from optical recordings.

claim: The average slope of ICa_opt was slower compared to INa (~500 µs vs. ~200 µs).
source: and slower compared to INa (~500 µs vs. ~200 µs, ICa_opt vs. INap<0.0001; Figure 6c,d).
evidence: This is based on experimental data from optical and electrical recordings shown in Figure 6c,d.

claim: The current mediating [Ca2+]i at the AIS resembles NaV channel kinetics.
source: Together, the findings indicate that the current mediating [Ca2+]i at the AIS resembles NaV channel kinetics.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data comparing kinetics.

claim: Whole-cell recording from HEK-293 cells transfected with SCN2A revealed Na+ currents in EGFP+ cells but not in non-transfected cells.
source: Whole-cell recording revealed Na+ currents in EGFP+ cells but not in non-transfected cells (average peak current density –115.7 ± 28.4 pA/pF, n = 10 vs. –3.7 ± 1.9 pA/pF at –20 mV, n = 5, respectively; Figure 7b).
evidence: This is based on experimental data from HEK-293 cells shown in Figure 7b.

claim: The inward currents in HEK-293 cells were completely abolished by 1 µM TTX (96.1 ± 1.3%).
source: The inward currents were completely abolished by 1 µM TTX (96.1 ± 1.3%, n = 7, one-tailed Wilcoxon matched-pairs signed rank test, p=0.0078, Figure 7c)
evidence: This is based on experimental data from HEK-293 cells shown in Figure 7c.

claim: The voltage-dependence of activation and inactivation revealed midpoints at –25.4 ± 2.1 mV and –74.1 ± 3.9 mV, respectively.
source: and the voltage-dependence of activation and inactivation revealed midpoints at –25.4 ± 2.1 mV and –74.1 ± 3.9 mV, respectively (n = 10, Figure 7d,e), consistent with previous work (Ben-Shalom et al., 2017), indicating a highly selective expression of NaV1.2 channels.
evidence: This is based on experimental data from HEK-293 cells shown in Figure 7d,e and supported by citation.

claim: An increase in ΔF/F was observed in every EGFP+ cell in response to a train of depolarizing pulses, indicating an influx of Ca2+.
source: We observed an increase in ΔF/F in every EGFP+ cell, indicating an influx of Ca2+ (average peak 0.46 ± 0.18% ΔF/F, range: 0.06–1.4% ΔF/F, n = 7; Figure 7f–h).
evidence: This is based on experimental data from HEK-293 cells shown in Figure 7f–h.

claim: Bath application of TTX revealed a significant decrease in the peak ΔF/F in HEK-293 cells (92.1 ± 3.8% reduction).
source: To test whether the [Ca2+]i increase required NaV channel opening we bath applied TTX (1 µM), revealing a significant decrease in the peak ΔF/F (92.1 ± 3.8% reduction, one-tailed Mann Whitney test, p=0.012, n = 4; Figure 7h).
evidence: This is based on experimental data from HEK-293 cells shown in Figure 7h.

claim: Molecular expression and opening of NaV1.2 channels suffices to mediate transmembrane Ca2+ influx.
source: The results indicate that molecular expression and opening of NaV1.2 channels suffices to mediate transmembrane Ca2+ influx.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the HEK-293 cell experiments.

claim: A peak conductance density of NaV channels of 16,000 and 850 pS µm–2 in the AIS and soma, respectively, reproduced the recorded AP and matched with AP-evoked Δ[Na+]i imaged in the AIS.
source: Based on multiple experimentally recorded parameters we constrained the model AP and found that a peak conductance density of NaV channels of 16,000 and 850 pS µm–2 in the AIS and soma, respectively, reproduced the recorded AP and matched with AP-evoked Δ[Na+]i imaged in the AIS (see Materials and methods and Figure 8a).
evidence: This is based on computational modeling constrained by experimental data shown in Figure 8a.

claim: Using calibrated ratiometric bis-Fura-2 imaging, Ca2+ entry though NaV channels induces a peak Δ[Ca2+]i of 55.6 nM during 1 AP.
source: Using calibrated ratiometric bis-Fura-2 (200 μM) imaging, we found that during 1 AP, Ca2+ entry though NaV channels induces a peak Δ[Ca2+]i of 55.6 nM (n = 4; Figure 8b, Figure 8—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on experimental data from ratiometric imaging shown in Figure 8b and Figure 8—figure supplement 2.

claim: ~36 nM is mediated by transmembrane Ca2+ entry via NaV channels (after accounting for ~35% from internal store amplification).
source: Since ~35% of AP-evoked Δ[Ca2+]i is caused by internal store amplification (Figure 2d) ~36 nM is mediated by transmembrane Ca2+ entry via NaV channels (Figure 8b).
evidence: This is based on inference from experimental data shown in Figure 2d and Figure 8b.

claim: When changing κs between 10–40 the gCa/gNa ratio was 0.38%.
source: When changing κs between 10–40 the gCa/gNa ratio was 0.38% (κs = 10: 0.37%, κs = 40: 0.39%; Figure 8c).
evidence: This is based on computational modeling shown in Figure 8c.

claim: The Δ[Ca2+]i from one AP reached a peak concentration of ~800 nM in the AIS.
source: The simulations showed that the Δ[Ca2+]i from one AP reached a peak concentration of ~800 nM in the AIS (Figure 9a,b).
evidence: This is based on computational modeling shown in Figure 9a,b.

claim: Due to the high density of NaV channels in the AIS they contribute to the majority of Δ[Ca2+]i and cause a rise of [Ca2+]i within submillisecond from the start of the AP (450 nM within <150 µs from AP threshold).
source: Due to the high density of NaV channels in the AIS they contribute to the majority of Δ[Ca2+]i and cause a rise of [Ca2+]i within submillisecond from the start of the AP (450 nM within <150 µs from AP threshold, red arrow in Figure 9b).
evidence: This is based on computational modeling shown in Figure 9b.

claim: Blocking both T- and L-type CaV channels significantly reduced the afterdepolarization and showed a trend to reduce the afterhyperpolarization (ADP, p=0.039 and AHP, p=0.055).
source: Blocking both T- and L-type CaV channels, contributing to ~27% to AP-evoked Ca2+ at the AIS (Figure 3), significantly reduced the afterdepolarization and showed a trend to reduce the afterhyperpolarization (ADP, p=0.039 and AHP, p=0.055, respectively, two-tailed paired t-tests, n = 5), without affecting other AP properties (p>0.30; Figure 9d and Table 1).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 9d and Table 1.

claim: When lowering [Ca2+]o with EGTA, the AP half-width significantly increased and the AHP was reduced (AP half-width, p=0.035 and AHP, p=0.043).
source: In contrast, when lowering [Ca2+]o with EGTA, which abolished all AIS Ca2+ influx (Figure 3), the AP half-width significantly increased and the AHP was reduced (AP half-width, p=0.035 and AHP, p=0.043, two-tailed paired t-tests, n = 4; Figure 9d, Table 1).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 9d and Table 1.

claim: NaV-mediated Ca2+ entry may act to open BKCa channels, thereby driving K+ efflux and facilitating axonal AP repolarization.
source: These results are consistent with the temporal differences in AP-evoked AIS [Ca2+]i and suggest that NaV-mediated Ca2+ entry may act to open BKCa channels (Figure 9e), thereby driving K+ efflux and facilitating axonal AP repolarization.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data and is speculative about the mechanism.

claim: Studies in the squid giant axon showed that an early component of depolarization-induced Ca2+ entry is tetrodotoxin (TTX)-sensitive and reflected a 1% conductivity of NaV channels for Ca2+ ions.
source: Our findings are in agreement with the depolarization-induced Ca2+ entry in the squid axon which is tetrodotoxin (TTX)-sensitive and reflected a 1% conductivity of NaV channels for Ca2+ ions (Baker et al., 1971).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: NaV channels in mammalian axons have a PCa/PNa ratio of 0.06.
source: If we assume there exists proportionality between permeability and conduction we can apply the equation of permeability ~ conductance/concentration × valency2 (Baker et al., 1971; Meves and Vogel, 1973). With our extracellular solutions [Ca2+]o/[Na+]o being 0.0148 and the valence ratio (Ca2+/Na+)2 being four we can calculate that NaV channels in mammalian axons have a PCa/PNa ratio of 0.06.
evidence: This is based on calculations using experimental data and equations from cited research.

claim: The calculated PCa/PNa value of 0.06 is in range of direct recordings for PCa/PNa in the sciatic nerve and squid axons (0.10 and 0.14).
source: Notably, the value is in range of direct recordings for PCa/PNa in the sciatic nerve and squid axons (0.10 and 0.14, Hille, 1972; Meves and Vogel, 1973)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Recordings from NaV1.5 channels revealed PCa/PNa ratios of ~0.04.
source: as well as recordings from NaV1.5 channels revealing PCa/PNa ratios of ~0.04 (Cruz et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Such permeability is orders of magnitude lower than PCa/PNa ratios of acetylcholine receptors or NMDA receptors (1.0 and 17, respectively).
source: Such permeability is orders of magnitude lower than PCa/PNa ratios of acetylcholine receptors or NMDA receptors (1.0 and 17, respectively) (Lewis, 1979; Iino et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Molecular dynamic studies of NaV channels showed that ionic interactions between Na+ and Ca2+ at the channel pore are complex.
source: Molecular dynamic studies of NaV channels showed that ionic interactions between Na+ and Ca2+ at the channel pore are complex (Corry, 2013; Boiteux et al., 2014; Naylor et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The energy barrier of the selectivity filter strongly favors Na+ ions but can be flexible, changing in conformational states and consistent with modest Ca2+ permeation.
source: The energy barrier of the selectivity filter strongly favors Na+ ions but can be flexible, changing in conformational states and consistent with modest Ca2+ permeation (Corry, 2013; Boiteux et al., 2014; Naylor et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: NaV channels are clustered to very high densities (~1000 channels µm–2) at the AIS and nodes of Ranvier.
source: Although the Ca2+ conductivity of the channels is small it achieves near–micromolar Ca2+ changes in axons as NaV channels are clustered to very high densities (~1000 channels µm–2) at the AIS and nodes of Ranvier (Neumcke and Stämpfli, 1982; Lorincz and Nusser, 2010; Kole and Stuart, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Nodes of Ranvier produced subthreshold-activated Ca2+ entry.
source: Consistent with this idea, our imaging experiments showed that also nodes of Ranvier produced subthreshold-activated Ca2+ entry (Figure 1 and Figure 4), suggesting that NaV channel mediated Ca2+ entry could play similar roles in these domains.
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 1 and Figure 4.

claim: The rapid opening of high densities of NaV channels may act as a trigger to amplify [Ca2+]i via the activation of ryanodine receptors, mediating ER store release of Ca2+ from the giant saccular organelle.
source: At the AIS, the rapid opening of high densities of NaV channels may further act as a trigger to amplify [Ca2+]i via the activation of ryanodine receptors, mediating ER store release of Ca2+ from the giant saccular organelle, which extends continuously along the AIS of thick-tufted L5 pyramidal neurons (Figure 2).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: In axons, a single AP will mostly lead to NaV-mediated Ca2+ entry while an increasing number of APs, or longer sustained depolarization, will lead to an accumulation of Ca2+ mediated by CaV channel activation.
source: The rapid inactivation of NaV channels compared to the slow inactivation of CaV channels will lead to voltage- and time-dependent changes in the relative contribution of NaV and CaV channels to [Ca2+]i. In axons, a single AP will mostly lead to NaV-mediated Ca2+ entry while an increasing number of APs, or longer sustained depolarization, will lead to an accumulation of Ca2+ mediated byCaV channel activation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data and is based on inference about channel kinetics.

claim: Ca2+ entry via CaV channels has been identified as a major contributor to Ca2+ entry in sciatic nerve or Purkinje axons during trains of APs or prolonged depolarization for hundreds of milliseconds.
source: Indeed, Ca2+ entry via CaV channels has been identified as a major contributor to Ca2+ entry in sciatic nerve or Purkinje axons during trains of APs or prolonged depolarization for hundreds of milliseconds (Callewaert et al., 1996; Zhang and David, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: In vivo recordings from L5 pyramidal neurons show that they typically fire sparsely and on average ~1–4 Hz.
source: However, in vivo recordings from L5 pyramidal neurons show that they typically fire sparsely and on average ~1–4 Hz (de Kock et al., 2007)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The half-width of axonal APs is about ~300 µs.
source: and the half-width of axonal APs is about ~300 µs (Kole et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: NaV-mediated Ca2+ entry may be the main source for activity-dependent [Ca2+]i in the excitable domains of axons under physiological conditions.
source: In this view, NaV-mediated Ca2+ entry may be the main source for activity-dependent [Ca2+]i in the excitable domains of axons under physiological conditions.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data and is based on inference about physiological conditions.

claim: One downstream target of submembranous axoplasmic [Ca2+]i may be regulation of NaV inactivation kinetics via their Ca2+/calmodulin domain at their C-terminus.
source: What could be the functional role of NaV-mediated Ca2+ entry in axon initial segments and nodes of Ranvier? One downstream target of submembranous axoplasmic [Ca2+]i may be regulation of NaV inactivation kinetics via their Ca2+/calmodulin domain at their C-terminus as has been demonstrated for multiple NaV subtypes, including NaV1.2 and NaV1.6 (Sarhan et al., 2012; Reddy Chichili et al., 2013; Ben-Johny et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research and is speculative about the functional role.

claim: BKCa channels are exclusively activated by P/Q-type CaV channels in cerebellar Purkinje neurons with short AP durations.
source: BKCa channels are exclusively activated by P/Q-type CaV channels in cerebellar Purkinje neurons with short AP durations (Womack et al., 2004)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: In rat chromaffin cells with wider APs, BKCa channels are coupled with the Q- and slower activating L-type CaV channels.
source: but in rat chromaffin cells with wider APs, BKCa channels are coupled with the Q- and slower activating L-type CaV channels (Prakriya and Lingle, 1999).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: In L5 pyramidal neurons BKCa activation shortens the duration of somatic APs from ~1 ms to ~600 µs.
source: Also in L5 pyramidal neurons BKCa activation shortens the duration of somatic APs from ~1 ms to ~600 µs (Yu et al., 2010; Bock and Stuart, 2016; Roshchin et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: NaV channels may provide both a precisely-timed voltage-dependent activation and a [Ca2+]i rise within 150 µs to rapidly open BKCa channels and shape axonal AP repolarization.
source: Considering the brief duration of axonal APs in the L5 pyramidal neurons (~300 µs, Kole et al., 2007) NaV channels may provide both a precisely-timed voltage-dependent activation, via Na+ current, as well as a [Ca2+]i rise within 150 µs (Figure 9), to rapidly open BKCa channels and shape axonal AP repolarization.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data shown in Figure 9 and is speculative about the mechanism.

claim: T- and L-type CaV channels are too slow to mediate somatic AP repolarization.
source: In agreement with this conjecture our data show that T- and L-type CaV channels are too slow to mediate somatic AP repolarization, leaving open the possibility that a NaV-BKCa channel nanodomain coupling provides the required Ca2+ signal.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data and is speculative about the mechanism.

claim: Two-photon Ca2+ uncaging experiments showed that the [Ca2+]i rise at the first node of Ranvier in L5 axons opens nodal BKCa channels to shorten the AP duration and facilitate the generation of high firing rates in the proximal axon.
source: Recent two-photon Ca2+ uncaging experiments already showed that the [Ca2+]i rise at the first node of Ranvier in L5 axons opens nodal BKCa channels to shorten the AP duration and facilitate the generation of high firing rates in the proximal axon (Roshchin et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Nodal BKCa channels in Purkinje axons play a role in augmenting the hyperpolarization following APs and facilitate recovery from NaV inactivation to prevent propagation failures.
source: Further downstream from the initiation site nodal BKCa channels in Purkinje axons play a role in augmenting the hyperpolarization following APs and facilitate recovery from NaV inactivation to prevent propagation failures (Hirono et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The dual permeation of axonal NaV channels for Na+ and Ca2+ ions may serve a common function; mediating the rapid electrical upstroke of the AP and via Ca2+ signaling activating K+ efflux to recover from inactivation and accelerating NaV channel availability for the next AP.
source: The dual permeation of axonal NaV channels for Na+ and Ca2+ ions may thus serve a common function; mediating the rapid electrical upstroke of the AP and via Ca2+ signaling activating K+ efflux to recover from inactivation and accelerating NaV channel availability for the next AP, representing a fine-tuning specifically to the needs of axonal AP generation and conduction fidelity.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data and is speculative about the functional significance.

claim: Sites with a-EPSP-evoked [Ca2+]i transients were all positive to ßIV spectrin (n = 15 AISs and 23 nodes from n = 15 axons).
source: Sites with a-EPSP-evoked [Ca2+]i transients were all positive to ßIV spectrin (n = 15 AISs and 23 nodes from n = 15 axons).
evidence: This is based on experimental immunostaining data.

claim: The length of synaptopodin fluorescence linearly scales with Ankyrin G length (y = 1.005 x – 0.95, r2 = 0.966, p<0.0001, n = 19).
source: The length of synaptopodin fluorescence linearly scales with Ankyrin G length. Red trace, linear regression fit with y = 1.005 x – 0.95, r2 = 0.966, ****p<0.0001, n = 19.
evidence: This is based on experimental immunostaining data shown in Figure 2b.
